[`52092e46a318`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/52092e46a3187de479033ff8f3b9c52884d411ba) · [log `d65e276b15d3`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/d65e276b15d357a53b718b9c93189eb8b2d87874c2e7aeb30d6bd948c4073c0a.jsonl.gz)

The brief's pipeline layout, readers first. verification/layout.py is the one place that knows where a job's specification and its result are: flat (verification/jobs/ID.json, verification/results/ID/), as all 986 are, or under the UTC day the id begins with (verification/jobs/YYYY/MM/DD/ID.json), with one overflow shard for an id without a date. A job is never moved, since the runner tests the commit that last touched its file; a result goes beside its job; identical duplicates resolve to the flat copy and differing ones are named by pipeline.py validate. The conductor loads the module only for the one question that needs it, so a copy of the loop's scripts in a checkout without it still answers the others.

### Keep an example's per-case records as one pack a folder, read in place; hold the records to a budget in check

[`60db5b9da4f1`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/60db5b9da4f1a36c219b0fe20e0a074b55ee1479) · [log `d65e276b15d3`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/d65e276b15d357a53b718b9c93189eb8b2d87874c2e7aeb30d6bd948c4073c0a.jsonl.gz)

The records' rule of VF-053 (the user's decision 5: seal the records, show 359 restores, then slim them by rule). A native-selector run writes two files for each admitted selector; over examples 340 to 359 that was 16,376 of the 22,103 files their records held, one folder with 2,865 entries. examples/tools/targets/case_pack.py keeps such a folder as cases.tar.gz beside where it was: the same bytes under the same names, written so that the same files give the same pack. The validator (native_selectors.validate_result) reads a case from the folder or from the pack and compares its digest either way, so a plain checkout checks every case as before and nothing has to be fetched from the private archive, which a public reader cannot read. A selector run packs its own output at its end.

Applied in one pass to examples 341, 345, 347, 354 and 359: 16,376 files became 45 packs (37.0 MB to 0.9 MB), the twenty examples' records went from 22,103 files to 5,772, and no folder has more than 1,000 entries. Shown: each of the five handoffs (workflow_handoff.py handoff NNN, and --revision fix for 354 and 359) is byte for byte what it was; the five sealed originals restored from the store with artifacts.py fetch equal the packed records file for file (case_pack.py verify --against, 16,376 members); with one packed case of 359 removed, and then with one byte of it changed, its record became ineligible (does not exist; different raw checker output) while the other 39 established results stayed, and matched again with the pack put back; validate_example.py passes for the five. Not cut: the bytes of the large per-execution files (execution.json, 125 MB in 319 files), which are few and read whole; what to keep of them is a question about the evidence, for the user.

The budget: sync.py check reports more than 50 loose per-case files in one cases/ folder as an error that names the command, and more than 2,000 files under one example's records/ or 1,000 entries in one folder as a warning (none of either now; 50 ms). It also warns at 100 commits on neither develop nor main. The checkpoint's scan now reads a gzip blob as what it opens to, every member and whatever follows the last, and refuses one that opens to more than 256 MiB: without that, a credential inside a pack would have left unseen (POLICY 3, so each kept verdict is worked out once more).

Also in this commit, from the brief's acceptance table and VF-053: a test that kills the collector (SIGKILL) with a result's folder wiped and again with the result written, and collects again, with the earlier result sealed before the wipe; the watcher's private analysis reads an occurrence its machine never held from the store alone (shown on a disk store; on the real restricted bucket it is the watcher's to run); prune_workspaces.py counts a file as recoverable when the archive holds its exact bytes verified in the store, and its tests no longer read the machine's own archive; both run skills have the watcher say, with each verdict or merge, what waits on a person. VF-053 records what was done against each of its needs and stays open for the user.

[`4484e5de5649`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/4484e5de5649c74a966323791193690aea085f08) · [log `5a355d2db29d`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/5a355d2db29dca8ac81486807f93db35329a894b0615fb23ea11d018716f1c38.jsonl.gz)

Part 1 of llm-dlc/loops/lib-architecture-fast-follow.md. Three readers of the checker's --json output answered differently for the same bytes: for the first established row of example 359's selector record with only wire_version changed to 999, the ordinary decoder refused it while the native-selector check read it as established and the benchmark scored it correct; a stated.bounds.complete of the string "false" was established through Python's truthiness; and a process that exited with 2 beside a verified payload was scored correct. lib/src/proof_wire.rs now owns what prove --json and equivalence --json print (the wire version, the envelope, the exit as the maximum over a run's rows), with the command line as its caller. lib/python/jvmcontract_io.py is the one Python reader, standard library only, and keeps three questions apart: whether the bytes decode, whether the process ended as the command ends, and (the consumer's own) whether the evidence qualifies, for which it offers typed access where a missing or mistyped field is unknown.

Switched to it: ordinary ingestion (checker_output.py keeps its names and reads through it; an unreadable outcome's reason now names what the reader refused), the live native-selector check, the validation of archived selector records, and lib/benchmark/run.py, which the solver comparison reads through. A benchmark case must print its one row; a kill, an unknown version, a mistyped decision field, exit 2 and an exit that contradicts the verdict earn no score, and a valid refutation is still correct at exit 1. A new selector row records its wire version and a new record names both rule files.

A regression check under --cache now says what it did with each changed helper as data (the outcome's helpers: callee, action, the proof's claim key and whether it was found in the cache, a summary's reads and facts, a reason code). The notes in the output are rendered from the decision, word for word what they were, and the proof cache stores the decisions with a result. build.py and economics.py read the data and fall back to the notes for an outcome from before the field; their patterns never matched the two notes a summary writes. sharedHelpers still means a helper proved equal on every input.

### Bind a proof to the class file a JVM loads: one selection in the checker, observed by a JVM, compared at launch

[`9b801632c2f8`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/9b801632c2f8bb2942cfd59d9a2ebdfbf0a3b4e7) · [log `5a355d2db29d`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/5a355d2db29dca8ac81486807f93db35329a894b0615fb23ea11d018716f1c38.jsonl.gz)

Part 2 of llm-dlc/loops/lib-architecture-fast-follow.md. Two JARs that differ only in how the manifest spells Multi-Release's value (one line, or folded over two) load different classes on JDK 17, 21 and 25: the versioned entry of the first, the base entry of the second. The preparation took the base class of both; the Python launch guard and the Rust checker bound to release 21 took the versioned class of both, so on the folded JAR the checker refuted a property the JVM satisfies. Three parties each had a rule; now there is one selection, and it is held to a JVM.

lib/src/classpath.rs: ClassPath::bind says which class file stands for a class name on an ordered class path and the bound runtime (provider, JAR entry, SHA-256, how it was selected, every candidate, later holders), or a typed refusal with the candidates' digests and origins; every reader of class bytes in the checker goes through it. The manifest is read as the JDK's reader reads it, measured with fifteen spellings: a spelling on which that reading and the JAR specification's differ is ambiguous, and a class with a versioned entry in such a JAR is refused unless JVMCONTRACT_CLASS_OBSERVATIONS says which class file a JVM of the bound release loaded; an observation of other bytes than the rule's is a refusal with both digests. jvmcontract class-bindings answers for every side and class of a launch in one process, with whether the bound class file declares a method asked about and which entry stands for each logical name of a JAR.

examples/tools/targets/class_binding.py: the Python tools select nothing by rule. A class with one class file is read as before, and its prepared record is unchanged. A class the original artifact holds several class files of is bound at preparation by LoadedClasses on each JDK the artifact runs on (classSha256, jarEntry, classObservation); JDKs that load different bytes, another code source, or bytes no class file has are refused with both digests. Parameter lookup and every reader of a prepared entry class take the bound entry (runtime.bound_class). The native launch guard asks the checker for its bindings, one process whatever the sides and classes, and compares provider and digest with the prepared ones; the equivalence route extracts a JAR by the checker's own logical entries. A native-selector task asks once, whatever its number of selectors. runtime_jar.effective_entries stays as an inventory view for the upgrade review's tools, with the measured rule.

Example 361 exercises the public DecimalConversion.fromBytes twice on the same buffer. Twelve original windows include signed values, nonzero positions, prefix and suffix bytes, and two scales. ### Prove independent cursors for duplicate heap buffers (verification pending)

[`098d10421441`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/098d104214419f0cc82826d07226e78aa08f008c) · [log `16a5ff56e823`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/16a5ff56e8239b2266188ade450c7ce7cb5ca71fa2be55fc21e0ef47a4b6c1ba.jsonl.gz)

On an exact heap buffer the native checker now runs the selected JDK duplicate, markValue and session bytecode. The new buffer shares the same array and inherits the mark, position, limit and capacity, while reads and position changes remain local. The existing boundary on foreign sessions still applies. A strict probe established the duplicate and bulk-read contract on symbolic bytes up to length six and all valid windows. The previous checker refused duplicate. A deliberately shared-cursor assertion was refuted, both Temurin 21 and 25 passed the focused regression, and all 49 selected test groups passed.

The domain pilot binds actual historical wrap operands and the identity of the returned buffer entering decimal conversion. At the user's request (2026-11-22), layout.WRITE goes from "flat" to "shards": a new job is written to verification/jobs/YYYY/MM/DD/ID.json and its result to verification/results/YYYY/MM/DD/ID/. Both folders had passed the 1,000 entries GitHub's web view lists (1,092 jobs, 1,122 results). Jobs written before stay flat, each result beside its job, and every reader already resolves both layouts through layout.py. VERIFY_LAYOUT=flat restores the old layout for one command.

The pipeline's tests assumed flat paths. test_pipeline.py gains Repo helpers (job_path, job_rel, indexed, collected) that resolve through layout.py, submit() takes an env, and every hand-built jobs/ or results/ path goes through them. test_layout.py's new-job check follows WRITE. test_capture.py plants its earlier results where the job's result goes. The README and layout.py docstring say what changed.

### Add a setup phase to single-agent runs: a setup agent prepares a brief, and its notes go into the brief

[`8c34dda527cf`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/8c34dda527cfdf5146519c7ca7657c32a10bd614) · [log `bc6875f19609`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/bc6875f196095accf06f10d226559e4a53f115a0aa1065c1fb8d58fc91367fb4.jsonl.gz)

single_run.py setup NAME --brief FILE starts a setup agent (Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort by default) whose two texts come from the new llm-dlc/loops/setup-agent-template.md, with the brief and its record filled in. The agent only fetches, pins, verifies and builds what the brief needs, records it, and ends its record with a '## Setup Agent Notes' section for the domain agent. single_run.py notes NAME [--to FILE] puts that section into the brief and any other copy of it, replacing an earlier one, so a second run changes nothing. The /single-agent-run skill gains --setup and a 'A setup phase' section (when to use it, the drift signals for answering stop, waiting on its jobs, and the handover to the domain run), and llm-dlc/README.md describes it.

The template carries the lessons of the first setup pass (2026-11-22, the Spring and Java data brief): a built-in way to wait on jobs, checked substitution for public repositories that have gone away (and no assuming that an artifact exists elsewhere), a private GNUPGHOME whose agent is stopped at the end, and that other sessions' memory notes are not instructions. Verified with three new tests in test_single_run.py (the template's texts, the notes section's extraction and replacement, and a real setup run on the stand-in client through to notes in two copies of a brief), and test_costs.py run --changed: test_single_run, test_brief_run, test_conductor, test_prove_loop and test_watch all pass.

[`44a802d5ada1`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/44a802d5ada1e5f3dc7d8802d0336b44d2a235a7) · [log `6b2889ccdaec`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/6b2889ccdaec35d0e89c08b53986e61ce963244469c3f164bc387dc26f712057.jsonl.gz)

The jbmc-java-semantics-gap run found that the native checker selected the first-declared interface default rather than the maximally specific one: example 382's dispatch was falsely refuted and firstDeclared falsely proved, both contradicted by the JVM (counterexample x=0). Fixed in stypsqmy; the brief's 98 statements and the conformance tests were rechecked and unchanged. VF-055 records it and leaves open an audit of earlier native verdicts that dispatch through library defaults. Also the watcher's decision single-jbmc-java-semantics-gap-D001 (continue: 13/13 historical JBMC-only claims, campaign 12/60 to 50/60). Documentation and decision record only.

### Redaction policy 7: Codex encrypted reasoning quoted in text

[`3735ae401384`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/3735ae40138474d38450035d1b1046268e004e0e) · [log `389ef8742209`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/389ef87422093e17a9fc5a7537591d3e625ea90e1d3f6db621462689d2a248e3.jsonl.gz)

Policy 6 removed Codex's encrypted reasoning under its own key (encrypted_content), but Astra quotes the same ciphertext in command arguments and tool output, where each blob stays a long-token warning that no evidence can vouch for (79 open in the jbmc-java-semantics-gap session alone). Policy 7 adds a text rule for its Fernet form, gAAAAA followed by at least 60 URL-safe base64 characters, with a cheap gate on the prefix. Like policy 6 it is not audited as a leak (UNAUDITED_KINDS), so logs stored before it keep their warnings instead of turning into errors. Test: test_codex.Redaction.test_encrypted_reasoning_in_text, made-up blob in a heredoc, in prose and in echoed JSON; idempotent; no warning left; a pre-policy log is not an error; short or embedded look-alikes are kept. ### Add a brief queue: briefs run one after the other, and the handover between them is one command

[`234bada26f96`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/234bada26f96d80a0b757eed339266b62811f7f0) · [log `50a9064dc1c7`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/50a9064dc1c7e895aa5c66c4bd3727668697b333a23d27f5ad79bb1f8b30a3f7.jsonl.gz)

llm-dlc/tools/brief_queue.py keeps the briefs a watcher runs in llm-dlc/loop-summaries/queue.json (gitignored) and logs every change to the committed llm-dlc/loops/queue.jsonl, so the queue no longer lives in one watcher's memory. Any session may add (with --first, --after or --before), move, remove or change a brief; a brief copied into ~/code/scripts/analysis/queue/ is added in file-name order. Each brief takes the defaults the user sent with every brief until now (an Opus 5.5 setup phase; Codex Astra 6.2 at max effort continuing the previous domain session; the 'aspirational' texts, now llm-dlc/loops/domain-prompt-aspirational.md), unless KEY=VALUE or a queue.KEY front-matter line overrides them. 'brief_queue.py next [--finished]' is the whole handover, recorded step by step so a failure or a crash resumes where it stopped: it commits the watcher's decisions, lands the run, checkpoints develop, clears failed jobs' work folders whose originals are remote_verified, moves the workspace onto the line, starts the next setup run, and after it lands the setup, puts its notes into both copies of the brief and starts the domain run. It never promotes main and never runs the default tests: the user decided on 2026-11-23 that both stay theirs. The /single-agent-run skill gains 'A queue of briefs' (the handover, the plateau rule the user chose: with a brief waiting, two cycles with no claim decided are a reason to stop, and what to do when a client refuses a session), and llm-dlc/README.md describes it.

Verified with llm-dlc/tools/test_brief_queue.py: three unit tests (front matter and settings, naming and placement, cleanup only of archived failed-job folders) and two tool tests that take briefs through real single-agent runs on the stand-in client: one from the inbox with a setup phase and one added with --no-setup, moved first, run, landed, checkpointed, setup notes put into both copies, and a failing step named and resumed. test_costs.py run --changed passes, and the tier lint agrees.

### Let a loop recover a working copy another session left stale, instead of ending

[`66a11552a2d0`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/66a11552a2d0f0e82714aa142956062bbf3cb652) · [log `50a9064dc1c7`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/50a9064dc1c7e895aa5c66c4bd3727668697b333a23d27f5ad79bb1f8b30a3f7.jsonl.gz)

feature-loop.sh reads @- (last_change) before and right after each turn, while its agent isn't working. When jj refuses there with "The working copy is stale", the loop now runs llm-dlc/tools/unstale.py, as CLAUDE.md tells an agent to, and says so in its log and summary. Then it reads @- again and goes on. If unstale.py can't recover (two copies with edits of their own), the loop stops with status 1 as before, and the log says a person is needed. Before this, the loop ended on the first refusal: on 2026-11-23 21:15 trusted-kernel's second cycle ended that way, before its verdict, after a turn that had gone well. The cause, in the operating notes' section on stale workspaces, is another workspace's sync.py rewriting commits this line is based on. The operating notes now say a loop recovers itself.

### Put verification jobs first in the machine's kill order, keep 8G free, and say when a job died of the machine's memory

[`6a95057202be`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/6a95057202be8817fdeb3f77e1de5cfa85555825) · [log `7a06980e99e0`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/7a06980e99e0e479a5b73e617e770038a5d37786e1130f839f0407fb21313790.jsonl.gz)

The user's rule (2026-11-24): should the machine run short of memory, no open tmux window, session, watcher or agent goes first; verification jobs do, and the agents then regroup. Every process had oom_score_adj 0, so a global OOM took the biggest process, whoever's (the watcher's window on 2026-11-22). An ordinary user can raise oom_score_adj but not lower it, and scopes refuse OOMScoreAdjust= on this systemd, so the order is made by raising: the step wrapper writes job_oom_score_adj (default 1000) to /proc/self/oom_score_adj, inherited by everything a step starts; test_costs.py run (and so default_run.py) joins at 500 (join_kill_order), as does the probe command in CLAUDE.md and the READMEs (choom -n 500); the rest keeps 0.

The runner also keeps memory_floor (default 8G, --memory-floor) free: no job starts that would take available memory under it, and when the machine falls under it anyway the runner SIGKILLs its newest job at once, one at a time. Such a job is cancelled (memoryStop in its result) and runs again when there is room; stopped a second time, counted across runners, it is out-of-memory for its submitter to regroup. A step's limitOoms (memory.events oom) tells a kill at the machine's end (0) from one at its own limit, and attention says which: more memory does not help the first. Documented in the result schema, verification/README.md, pipeline.toml, the run-verification skill and a new operating-notes section, The kill order when memory runs out, with how to regroup.

### Merge oom-order: jobs first in the kill order, 8G kept free

[`0407daf7df36`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/0407daf7df360f3c16a58bae92a45355f5818261) · [log `7a06980e99e0`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/6c5c7798-21e3-46a5-b989-5313736bdc7f/7a06980e99e0e479a5b73e617e770038a5d37786e1130f839f0407fb21313790.jsonl.gz)

Merges the advisor's oom-order workspace (oytomkyp, at the user's request): verification jobs run at oom_score_adj 1000, so the kernel kills them before tests and sessions. The runner keeps 8G of the machine free, stopping and requeuing once its newest job when the machine falls below that. Results now say when a job died of the machine's memory rather than its own cap. CLAUDE.md's probe command gains choom, and the operating notes gain 'The kill order when memory runs out'. The one conflict was lib/tests/costs.json, where both sides changed the per-file test counts: resolved by keeping the brief-generation side's rows with oom-order's test_pipeline counts, then regenerating with test_costs.py estimate; lint agrees. The 41 test files the merge changed passed under an 8G cap (test_costs.py run --changed --from ktpoosql). No runner was up, so the new kill order applies from the runner's next start.

### 4. 2026-11-15 17:38 UTC

> I like chaining the sessions because future sessions learn implicitly from previous sessions -- this is by design. I think auto compaction is probably the way to go. If we hit auto compact without a commit, then it requires user input. In theory, this should only happen in earlier cycles as later cycles benefit from the foundation that was previously built. I don't like adding any extraneous information to moonshot input because it defeats the purpose of experimenting. I am thinking 600k is a reasonable limit. Can this be updated while the current loop is running so as not to disrupt it?

**Reply:**

No, the running loop can't pick up the change. Its bash parsed the whole cycle loop when it started, so nothing written to the script now reaches it. But you can apply the change at a cycle boundary without losing anything. I've made the change and committed it in the side workspace `moonshot`, where it can't touch the loop's working copy.

## The change (`uzporttn`)
- **600k limit:** every moonshot turn passes `--autocompact 600k`. Briefs are left alone because they have their own stopping rules. `FEATURE_LOOP_AUTOCOMPACT` overrides the value; claude accepts 100k to 1M.
- **Compaction with no commit stops the loop:**
  - The loop watches the instruction turn for an automatic compaction. If no commit has landed since the cycle began, or since the previous compaction, it ends the turn right there, which is between model calls, and stops claude's child processes too.
  - It then writes "Stopped …: cycle N (item X) compacted with no commit at T tokens; session … needs attention" to the run record and exits.
- **Unchanged:** sessions stay chained across cycles, and the moonshot prompt gets nothing added. Manual `/compact` turns and the end-of-run summary turn aren't watched.
- **Stats:** `loop_stats.py` counts this as a new stop reason, "compacted, no commit".

**How I tested it:** I put a stand-in `claude` on PATH that emits a compaction event.
- Auto compaction with no commit: the turn ended immediately, no child process was left behind, and the stop reason was written.

> Make a note for conductor brief -- we will likely want a moonshot conductor, that makes some qualitative judgment on compact (i.e., whether it's compacting because the work is really hard but still making good progress, or whether stuck and requiring human input) and acts on it. This judgment should come from outside of the primary moonshoot loop so as not to distract it and seems like a good fit
>
> *… (shortened; the log has the full text)*

**Reply:**

I've added the moonshot conductor to the conductor brief as **Design 7** and **plan step 7**, committed as `ulzlppqm` in the `stream-conductor` workspace with a plain `jj commit`. The current loop keeps running untouched.

**What the brief now says:**
- **The problem:** a moonshot has no acceptance criteria. Sessions stay chained by design, the one-line input gets nothing added, and leaving an item unfinished is fine if the work was productive, since a later pass can return to it.
- **The judgment:** at each automatic compaction, a separate session outside the moonshot loop decides whether the work is hard but still going well, or stuck and needing a person. It reads the transcript, the commits and diff, test runs, jobs, and whether the same failure keeps coming back. Keeping it outside means the moonshot isn't distracted, which fits the conductor's purpose.
- **The actions:** by default it lets the turn go on. If the session is stuck, it stops the loop and queues a decision for you saying why. The brief leaves other actions for the implementer to propose, such as ending the item at its last good commit. Every judgment goes into the decision record with its reasoning.
- **The fallback:** the mechanical stop in `uzporttn` (600k limit, stop on a compaction with no commit) applies when the conductor isn't running or can't decide. The brief notes that `show_progress` already sees the compaction event and holds claude's process id, so that's where the hand-off goes.

### 26. 2026-11-16 03:29 UTC

> Should we relax the 1GB memory limit? This can easily go to 4GB (or higher), especially as real world changes can be much more complex

**Reply:**

Yes, I'd relax it, but for one-off probes only, and with a hard cap. Some background first.

**Where the 1 GB comes from:** it isn't a limit in the checker. It's the line in `CLAUDE.md:20` (repeated in `verification/README.md:57`) between what an agent may run during its turn and what it must queue as a verification job. The checker itself can already use much more as a job. The trouble is that the agent's quick probes must stay under 1 GB, so it ends up tuning memory to pass that line before it knows whether the real proof works. That's what happened at 03:12–03:16.

To be fair, the two fixes it made there would matter at any limit: 32k fresh variables for every store into an unknown array, and dense per-path models. Real changes would hit both. But the next round of that kind of tuning would mostly be work to satisfy the rule.

**What I'd change:**
1. **Agent probes:** a single inline run of the checker may use up to **4 GB and a few minutes**, inside a `systemd-run` scope with `MemoryMax=4G`. The agent already runs its probes in such scopes, so the cap is easy to enforce. During 286 one of them was killed for running out of memory at its 2 GiB cap, and the loop carried on unharmed.
2. **Tool-tier tests stay at 1 GB.** The default run starts many tests at once, so 4 GB each would overrun the loop's memory. Real-world-sized proofs stay as jobs, as now.
3. **Jobs** need no change. They already declare their memory, and the runner has 80G while one loop runs.

> Go ahead and implement your recommended changes, considering the timing and safety points you raised

**Reply:**

The new probe limit is in place and the loop is unaffected. It takes effect from cycle 4: the running cycle 3 process loaded `CLAUDE.md` when it started and won't reload it.

**The rule** (commit `upkxonlz`, in `CLAUDE.md` with the same text in `verification/README.md`):
- A single run of a prover or model checker on one claim may now run inline, one at a time, for up to **5 minutes and 4 GB**.
- It has to run under a cap it can't exceed: `systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=4G -p MemorySwapMax=0 timeout 300 COMMAND`. The agent already ran its probes this way, with a 2G cap.
- The rule tells agents not to tune memory or time just to fit under the cap. A run that needs more is still a job.
- The default test run and the tool tier keep their 1 GB.

**How I landed it:**
- **Commit:** made in the `moonshot` workspace as a plain `jj commit`, so the loop's working copy was never touched. The `moonshot` workspace is back on uzporttn.

**Reply:**

Everything is pushed and published. `main` and `origin/main` both point at `nvsxqxwk` ("Record session traces"), so no commit on the default line is left behind. The push's check reported 0 errors and 0 warnings, and it uploaded the outstanding session traces. The working copy is empty, so the skill can start.

**`--unattended`** tells the skill you're away for the whole run. It's meant for runs over examples named by number.
- The skill doesn't wait for your approval of each example's claims. It still prints them, checks each against the example's summary and advisory, and accepts them for you when they say no more than the catalog entry does.
- Each claim it accepts this way is recorded as a decision flagged for your later review.
- An example whose claims it isn't sure of is left out of the run and named in the final report, waiting for you.
- Anything else it can decide itself, it decides and records instead of asking. Anything that only you can decide still waits for you, and the rest of the run carries on around it.

**`--record-as NAME`** files the run under an existing loop's name, so its run record and statistics continue that loop's list. With `--record-as prove-examples`, 288 onwards adds to the same record and statistics as 285–287 instead of starting a new loop name.

The command to start the run:
```
/prove-java-change --unattended --record-as prove-examples continue session a4ac2b6c-a5b9-4507-a21e-1b56ae8b2c31: 288 289 290
```

| Context while working | median 257k, p90 414k | median 272k, p90 519k |

**Why waiting is so cheap**
- **Proof jobs don't wait in the session.** When the loop leaves an example to wait on its jobs, no Fable tokens are spent. The session only waits while a cycle is still running.
- **What it does wait on is mostly the inline default test run.** The most common waiting calls are polls of that run's log, then checks of the verification queue. Queuing the default run as a job, as I recommended earlier, would remove most of that $8.
- **No cache rebuilds.** No call wrote more than 100k tokens back into the cache. Gaps never let the cache expire, so a wait costs one small poll, not a full context rewrite.

**Cost and quality by context size**

| Context | $ per call | Cache reads' share of cost | Tool error rate |

**Reply:**

I agree: run the full suite as a non-blocking job on every merge, and make publishing the only point that waits for a clean result. Here's how I'd build it, with a few more ideas in the same spirit. I'll leave the loop to its own judgment.

### The core design

1. **Queue the default run as a pipeline job, tied to a commit.**
   - Every merge, and every example's last commit, queues `default tests at <change>`, a job that runs `test_costs.py run` and nothing else.
   - It runs in a throwaway jj workspace checked out at that commit, not in the live working copy. The result then belongs to that exact revision, and the loop's ongoing edits can't change what is tested halfway through.
   - Low priority (`nice`, a few CPUs), so it doesn't slow the proof jobs, which matter more.
2. **Nothing waits for it.** The session or watcher that queued it carries on. Its result comes back like any other job, through `wait`.
3. **The watcher triages failures:**
   - **Small and mechanical** (a test-inventory or lint row, a stale index, a doc count): the watcher fixes it in the side workspace, and the fix is merged at the next boundary between examples. The proving session never sees it.
   - **In the area the loop is working on** (the engine, the example's tools): the watcher writes a short note next to `expert-review.md`, for example `test-findings.md`, naming the failing test, the commit, and the commits since the last pass. The next cycle can read it.
   - **Anything else** goes to you.

It runs at low priority and keeps its compiled Rust build between runs. The job file can be committed from any workspace, and nothing waits for it.
- **Only the newest runs:** if a newer default-run job is waiting or running when one starts, it exits within seconds and its log says `default tests: superseded by ID`.
- **The watcher triages results:** `watch.py wait` reports each run that comes in, with its commit and the files that failed. Small mechanical failures I fix in the side workspace. Failures in the loop's own area go into a `test-findings.md` file the next cycle can read. Anything else comes to you.
- **The push gate:** `sync.py push` now refuses unless a passed run covers the commit being pushed. That's a run at the same commit, or at an earlier one whose only differences are files no test reads: traces, decisions, job results. `--skip-tests REASON` is there for you to override it.

| Option | What happens | Cost if wrong |
|---|---|---|
| **Accept** | The loop proves the claims as written | If you meant a different claim: a new setup session restates it, and the proofs are redone. Results on the old claim stay valid but answer a question you didn't ask. |
| **Hold** | The example sits out the run until you read the claims | One run's progress on that example, and nothing else |

The watcher now merges each stream into the default line the moment it finishes, and the merge loop is gone. The rehearsal commits are gone from the line. The full default test run passed on the result: 52 of 52 test files. Nothing is pushed.

**How a run works now**
- When a stream finishes (done, or left blocked), `run-streams.sh` asks the watcher to merge it right away, while the other streams keep running. If nobody answers within 30 minutes, the stream stays unmerged.
- The watcher answers by running `brief_run.py merge BRIEF STREAM`, which:
  - merges the stream's commits into the default line;
  - copies over its session logs;
  - closes the inbox items it acknowledged;
  - answers the question and records the merge in the main brief's Progress;
  - commits all of it.

  The brief's status becomes `done` once every stream is merged and done. If one was left blocked, the status says `blocked: stream S: …`.
- **Conflicts:** a merge that conflicts in real work is taken back. The skill tells the watcher to resolve small, clear conflicts by hand, as the `/prove` watcher does between examples, and otherwise answer `leave` and tell you.
- **After a merge:** the watcher runs the default test run, unless the brief rules tests out. It reports a failure to you rather than fixing it.
- **Without a watcher** nothing is merged, and the end of the run prints the command for each stream.

## The `land` gap

`land` brings the foundation's commits onto the default line, and `merge` now does the same for each stream. It takes one of two paths:

- **Moved forward**, when the line hasn't moved since the workspace was made. It rebases the default working copy onto the workspace's tip.
- **Merged**, when the line has moved. It makes a merge commit, regenerates the trace files and commits.

The rehearsal took the forward path, and two things went wrong:

1. **No session logs. Fixed in `krtsppoly`.** Only the merge path ran `sync.py regenerate`, which copies the logs a workspace lacks. The forward path didn't, so `check` reported the foundation's log missing until I ran `adopt-logs`. `land` now runs `adopt-logs` on both paths.

2. **Trace files that belong to no session. Not fixed.** After the landing, the default working copy held regenerated trace files (`index.json`, the traces README, metrics, and the summaries of my session and the verification loop's). jj's operation log shows `sync.py` rewriting the default workspace's working-copy commit as "Record session traces" at 02:49:00, 02:49:24 and 02:49:38, while the foundation was finishing and before `land` ran. - **The cause:** the run's starting point is recorded as a jj change id, the merge that landed run 5 (`ormsxnzy`). Since nothing has been pushed, `sync.py commit` rewrote that commit at 23:27 to add trace lines, as it always does with unpushed commits. Then at 00:35 the agent put a bookmark (`external-upgrade-evaluation-v0`) on the old copy as its frozen V0 baseline. Both copies are now visible, so the id is ambiguous, the lookup fails, and the commit list comes back empty.
- **What it affects:** only the counts in my summaries and in the agent's end-of-cycle report. When the cycle ends, I'll judge from its report and the actual log, not from the empty list. Landing doesn't use that list.
- **Left alone:** I didn't touch the agent's bookmark, because it's part of its work. Whether the bookmark should outlive the run is in VF-049 for you to decide.
- **The forgotten workspaces:** jj also forgot 7 old workspaces at 23:24, including the `domain-advances-*` ones. Their folders were already gone, so nothing was lost.

The commit check's warnings are now 12 copies of the same pending log-filename false positive, which waits on your approval of 21903e4c. I'm still watching.

It's 5.4 MB compressed but opens to 267 MiB, just over the 256 MiB the checkpoint will decompress to scan for secrets.

**What cycle 1 achieved:**
- **Both Guava methods proved independently.** A separate Rust checker proved `Ints.indexOf` and `Longs.indexOf` straight from Guava's release class files. The claim holds for every legal array length and target: each call returns the first match or -1 and leaves the heap unchanged. Each proof is about 1.1 KB and checks in about 1.2 ms.
- **The transfer was cheap.** Moving from `Ints` to `Longs` took 49 net lines of code, reusing the same induction argument.
- **The controls work:**
  - All six deliberately broken versions of the method were caught with checked counterexamples.
  - Lean independently proved the scalar identity.
  - The LRAT proof checker certified all 18 observed UNSAT solver calls.
  - The optional range-fill case (example 337) found a counterexample on a real JVM.
- All 9 jobs passed.

**Why one more cycle:** the agent recommends extending the checker to `Arrays.fill`'s write frame. But the brief makes that recommendation conditional on showing that a deliberately corrupted version of the existing prover can no longer get a false claim accepted. The agent says that measurement is still missing, and 337's original any-length result is still unresolved. Both are in scope for this brief. If cycle 2 closes them, or shows they can't be closed, I'll move on to receiver-construction.

**Reply:**

Beyond-jbmc's blind first pass caught the native checker giving a wrong answer, and that bug will get a finding.

**What went wrong:** on Sisu Plexus, the checker claimed a counterexample that the JVM refutes. It renames the old version's classes into a package called `before.` when comparing versions, and that renaming leaked into a value the program can see. The old version's `toString()` came back with `before.` in its class name, so the two versions looked different when they aren't. The advisor spotted it. It's the same kind of soundness bug as VF-055: an accepted result the JVM refutes.

**What the agent has done:** it recorded the miss as an incorrect native decision in the blind scoring, which keeps the blind count honest. It hasn't fixed the cause or opened a finding for it.

**What I'll do:** if it's still unfixed when the cycle ends, I'll add VF-062 after the run lands. It will say the fix needs a control that renames nothing the program can see. I'm not writing `findings.md` mid-run, because the last landing conflicted on that file and we'd both pick the same number. I've saved this in memory and told the advisor.

**Rest of the blind pass**, as the advisor read it:
- the workflow reached a public method in 12 of 16 projects;
- it decided none of the 16 main questions on its own;
- given the reference caller, the native checker proved Cactoos' sticky scalar.

Disk is at 64 GB free and dropping as jobs write results; I'll clean up when the cycle ends.

**Reply:**

Case B (Apache POI #1420) is blocked at startup too, committed as zqtzzskx. Initializing POI's `DataFormatter` starts Log4j's `StatusLogger`, which reads all the system properties at once through `System.getProperties()`. The checker can only record properties read one at a time by name, so it refuses.

That makes two cases out of two whose public call is blocked by what a library does at startup:
- **ThreeTenBP:** a reflective `Method` held in a field.
- **POI:** logging that reads every system property.

For the product, this is the clearest pattern so far: startup state left by common libraries (logging, locale handling, reflection) stands between a PR's URL and a verdict. It's reusable and worth fixing in the checker. I've added it to the product notes, and I'll put it in a finding if the run doesn't address it.

**Reply:**

The 20-cases setup finished 19 of its 20 cases in about 55 minutes, so I've answered stop. The 20th, Calcite (J12), is waiting on a resubmitted build. Calcite has a build plugin that reads git metadata, and it can't read the setup's shallow checkout, so the new job turns that plugin off. Its result gets collected as soon as it's back, and the domain agent picks J12 up from there. Spending another setup cycle just to wait for one job isn't worth it.

**For the product:**
- **Shallow clones** break build plugins that read git metadata. Intake needs a list of such plugins to turn off, or a deeper clone.
- **When a project's build can't run here,** the setup compiled just the changed files against the released jar instead. This fallback worked every time and is reusable. Five builds couldn't run:
  - J08 needs a Thrift binary that isn't installed;
  - J15, J18 and J20 depend on repo.spring.io, which now refuses access;
  - J19 needs plugins that aren't on any public repository.
- **Releases often don't match either side** of a PR, or already include the fix. A product has to name the exact jar for each side rather than assume.

*… (shortened; the log has the full text)*

The 20-cases brief finished in one cycle of about 90 minutes, so I stopped it.

**What it established:**
- **All 20 PRs** went through the frozen checker with no changes to it.
- **Behaviour changes:** 19 PRs showed a change a caller can see. Eclipse Collections kept its behaviour across all 127 collision subsets.
- **Questions decided:** 43 across 85 histories. 42 were established and 1 was refuted.
- **Jobs:** all 25 passed. Cached reruns reused 65 of 86 claim sides and agreed with fresh runs every time.

**A finding that may be a real Lucene bug (J14):** the refuted question isn't a checker failure. Lucene's fixed comparator still guesses a missing child from the whole parent block. So a child that the filter excluded, even one with a real value, still changes the parent's sort key, and the JVM confirms it.

Two other boundaries came up:
- Parquet's reused page writer keeps stale data after a fallback: 0 of 1,000 values decoded correctly, while the public file writer is fine.
- Kryo's wire length includes the enum's class name.

**Why stop:** the brief's outcome is reached. The one remaining item is a small check of whether the seven cases built on the fallback (the changed files compiled against the release jar) affect any result. The next brief, beyond-jbmc on the scaffold-first prompt, goes after the product's main gap (VF-063), so it's worth more.

**For the product:** after a 55-minute setup, each PR took about 4.5 minutes, the best throughput so far.
